ml.tagline: Teaching machines the chemistry of surfaces

demos.label: Try active learning
demos.caption: Your turn to find the best catalyst. A hidden curve gives the activity of every alloy composition, and each point you reveal costs one calculation. Tap the plot to run one yourself, or let the AI choose: it fits a Gaussian process to what it has seen (orange line, with its uncertainty as the shaded band) and runs next where the expected improvement is highest. This is the strategy behind our active-learning search that found Cu–Al for CO₂ reduction. The model is computed live in your browser; the hidden curve is a stand-in for DFT.

demos.label: Adsorption search
demos.caption: An adsorption search like the ones our models run. Eight starting placements of CO on a Cu(111) surface are relaxed with forces predicted by a graph neural network, and the lowest-energy site is kept. A DFT relaxation takes hours; a trained network takes a tiny fraction of that, so thousands of surfaces can be searched. Schematic: positions and energies are illustrative.

demos.label: Message passing
demos.caption: How a graph neural network reads a catalyst: each atom gathers information from its neighbours, one shell per layer, before the network predicts an energy. Tap any atom to start there.

overview: Finding a better catalyst means knowing how molecules bind to thousands of possible surfaces. Density functional theory (DFT) answers that one surface at a time, and each calculation takes hours to days, so whole families of materials stay unexplored.

We train machine-learning models on DFT data so they can stand in for the calculation: graph neural networks that read a catalyst as a graph of atoms and predict energies almost instantly, active learning that decides which DFT calculation to run next, and generative and multi-objective search that proposes new candidates instead of only ranking known ones.
Predictions go back to the lab. Candidates our models rank highly are made and tested with our collaborators, and the new results feed the next round of training.

dft.tagline: Following reactions one atom at a time

demos.label: Minimum energy path
demos.caption: A nudged-elastic-band (NEB) calculation running live in your browser. A chain of images slides downhill on a model energy surface (Müller–Brown, with minima A, B and C) until it traces the minimum-energy path; the climbing image then settles on the saddle point, the transition state, whose height above the start is the barrier. Pick other end points, change the number of images or the spring, and drag to turn the surface. We run the same method with DFT on real catalyst surfaces.

demos.label: Atom hop on Cu(111)
demos.caption: CO hopping between hollow sites on a three-layer Cu(111) slab, crossing a transition state each time. Schematic, not a computed trajectory.

overview: Density functional theory tells us how strongly molecules bind to a surface and how high the barriers are between them. From those numbers we build reaction networks and micro-kinetic models that predict which product a catalyst makes, and how fast.

Real electrocatalysis happens in water, under an electric field, with ions close by. We model these interfaces with explicit solvent, cations and applied potential, so that calculated mechanisms can be compared with what is measured.
Most of our DFT work is done with experimental groups around the world: we explain what they see, and predict what to make next.

dft.limitations: DFT is accurate to roughly a tenth of an electron-volt and becomes expensive for large or dynamic systems, which is why we pair it with machine learning and always compare with experiment.
